teaser: Count a beat, find a pattern, and make a rhythm of your own.
title: How Rhythm Is Math
question: How can counting turn into music you can feel?
idea: A steady beat gives us places to count, and rhythm makes patterns across those places.

curiosity.intro: A soft boom through the wall, a steady count, and a pattern to discover.
curiosity.carryForward: Keep the beat going, even when one count is quiet.

questions.question: What makes a beat feel steady?
questions.notice: Find Little listening to the drum and feeling the gentle pulse in their chest.
questions.say: A beat is the steady pulse underneath a rhythm. A heartbeat can remind us what a pulse feels like, although a real heart speeds up and slows down. It is steady-ish, not a perfect metronome.
questions.try: Put a hand on your chest for a quiet moment. Then tap a table at your own comfortable, even speed.

questions.question: Why does ONE help us find our place?
questions.notice: Watch Big and Little clap while four small beat marks repeat nearby.
questions.say: Musicians group beats so they can find their place. In 4/4 time, each bar has four beats: ONE, two, three, four. A stronger ONE can mark the start of the next group. Many songs use four, but not every song does.
questions.try: Clap four even beats. Make ONE a little louder, then repeat the group.

questions.question: Can silence belong inside a rhythm?
questions.notice: One piano key glows on ONE while the other counted beats stay quiet.
questions.say: Yes. A rest is a counted place of silence. The beat keeps moving underneath it. Sound on counts one, two, and four with silence on three still makes a four-beat rhythm.
questions.try: Clap one, clap two, stay silent on three, and clap four. Keep your counting steady.

questions.question: How can four boxes hold a rhythm?
questions.notice: Each box on the beat card holds one clap or one rest symbol.
questions.say: Rhythm is a pattern of sounds and silences across a beat. It can use long and short sounds, claps and rests, then repeat. Musicians are pattern detectives: they count, group, notice, and repeat.
questions.try: Draw four boxes. Put CLAP or REST in each one, play the row, and teach it to someone.

reading.title: Count the rhythm you can feel
reading.coverText: A beat gives rhythm a steady path through time.
reading.foldableNote: Carry a four-beat pattern in a small book.
reading.parentNote: Grade 3 reading. Welcome spoken answers and dictation. Clap the examples slowly enough that the count stays comfortable.

beats.title: A beat nearby
beats.passage: Boom-tap-tap-tap came softly through the wall. Little Wonderer put a hand on their chest. A heartbeat was already making a steady-ish pattern. It was not a perfect clock, but it offered a gentle clue: rhythm begins when sounds or movements meet a pulse we can feel.
beats.prompt: Why is a heartbeat only a gentle clue for a beat?

foldable.heading: A beat nearby
foldable.body: A drum sounded through the wall. Little felt a heartbeat too. It was steady-ish, not a perfect clock, but it offered a clue.

beats.title: A tick to count
beats.passage: Big tapped the table evenly. Little counted, “One, two, three, four.” Each number landed on a steady tick. That steady pulse was the beat. The claps could change, but the beat kept giving them places in time. Count was the tool that helped both Wonderers stay together.
beats.prompt: What stays steady while the claps change?

foldable.heading: A tick to count
foldable.body: Big tapped evenly while Little counted. Each number landed on a steady beat. Counting helped them stay together.

beats.title: Four make a bar
beats.passage: Musicians often gather beats into groups. In 4/4 time, one bar holds four beats. Little clapped ONE, two, three, four, making ONE a little louder. The stronger first beat pointed to the start of the group. Not every song uses four, but this group was easy to find again.
beats.prompt: What does the louder ONE help a musician find?

foldable.heading: Four make a bar
foldable.body: In 4/4 time, one bar has four beats. A louder ONE can show where the group begins again.

beats.title: Steady steps
beats.passage: Four even beats felt balanced, like walking left-right-left-right. At the piano, Little played one key on every beat. Next came a key only on ONE, then keys on one and three. The sounds moved around, yet Big’s quiet count stayed steady underneath them.
beats.prompt: How can the sounds move while the beat stays steady?

foldable.heading: Steady steps
foldable.body: Four beats felt balanced, like left-right-left-right. The sounds changed, but the quiet count stayed steady underneath.

beats.title: Pattern detectives
beats.passage: Rhythm was the pattern placed across the beat: long or short, clap or rest, sound or silence, then repeat. A rest was not a lost beat. It was a beat of silence that still had to be counted. Little clapped one, two, rested on three, and clapped four.
beats.prompt: Why does a rest still need to be counted?

foldable.heading: Pattern detectives
foldable.body: Rhythm uses sounds and silences across a beat. A rest is counted silence, not a lost beat. Patterns can repeat.

beats.title: Teach your rhythm
beats.passage: Little drew four boxes on a beat card. Each box held CLAP, pat, or rest. Then Little played the whole row and taught it to Big. Big repeated it. Rhythm was counting they could feel. Together they had become pattern detectives: count, group, notice, repeat.
beats.prompt: What makes a four-beat pattern easy to teach?

foldable.heading: Teach your rhythm
foldable.body: Little filled four boxes with CLAP, pat, or rest, played the row, and taught the pattern to Big.

math.title: Pattern detectives at practice
math.intro: Each sequence grows by the same step. Find the one missing count.
math.actionLabel: Find the next or missing count

tasks.prompt: Little’s clap counts grow by 2 each time. Which count comes next?
tasks.worked: 7 + 2 = 9, so the next clap count is 9.
tasks.label: TASK 1

tasks.prompt: Big marks every other count in a repeating rhythm. Which count is missing?
tasks.hint: Start at 2 and add 2 each time.
tasks.label: TASK 2

tasks.prompt: A stack of beat cards grows by 5 each time. Which total comes next?
tasks.label: TASK 3

tasks.prompt: Little counts pattern cards in steps of 5. Which total is missing?
tasks.hint: Add 5 after 15 and check that one more step reaches 25.
tasks.label: TASK 4

tasks.prompt: Practice taps are counted in steps of 10. Which total comes next?
tasks.label: TASK 5

tasks.prompt: Big counts all the claps from several rounds in steps of 10. Which total is missing?
tasks.label: TASK 6

math.extension: Make a new count-by-2, count-by-5, or count-by-10 rhythm sequence with one blank.
math.printNote: Write one number in each blank, then explain the step you found.
math.parentNote: Grade 2 math. Six skip-counting patterns use steps of 2, 5, and 10. Each sequence has exactly one missing number.
math.answerKeyIntro: Grade 2 math. Find the constant step, then add it to reach the next term or fill the gap.

writing.title: Write a rhythm someone can follow
writing.intro: Choose a scene. Say your pattern first, then draw or write it.
writing.draw: Draw four boxes. Fill each box with CLAP, pat, or rest.

frames.hint: say CLAP, pat, or rest four times
tell how someone can follow your beat

writing.check: Does your pattern have four places? Read or dictate each place in order.
writing.parentNote: Offer dictation: say each beat aloud while the child points to a box. Speech, drawing, invented spelling, or a written sentence all count.

questions.prompt: How many beats are in one bar of 4/4 time?
choices: Every song has a different answer
questions.answer: One bar of 4/4 time has four beats.
A rest is a counted place of silence, so the beat keeps moving.

choices: A pattern of sounds and silences
questions.answer: Rhythm is a pattern of sounds and silences across a beat.

parentGuidance: A beat is a steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern placed across it. A heartbeat is only a gentle analogy because real heart rate changes and is not a metronome. In 4/4 time there are four beats per bar, often with a stronger first beat, but not every song is in four. A rest is counted silence. Clap and table-tap freely; an optional piano activity needs only one ordinary key and a grown-up nearby. The scenes are not measured music notation. Welcome speech, dictation, drawing, movement, or writing, and stop when the shared play feels complete.
